"I will write my own book and then you will come to know everything."Sonia Gandhi's response to former external affairs minister Natwar Singh's explosive autobiography in 2014 was as much a promise as it was a rebuttal. Singh's book had stirred a political storm with its account of why she declined the prime minister's post after the Congress-led UPA won the 2004 general elections. More controversially, he claimed that Rahul Gandhi had strongly opposed his mother's elevation, fearing she could meet the same fate as her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, and mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, both of whom were assassinated. Sonia, who had publicly attributed her decision to her "inner voice", was now promising to tell her side of the story.Twelve years later, that promise has come full circle. Sonia Gandhi's memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, was released on November 10, bringing her own account of her life, family and political journey into the public domain. The book has already triggered political reactions and renewed debate over some of the most contentious episodes involving the Gandhi family.But Sonia is hardly the first political figure to find that putting personal recollections on paper can have consequences far beyond the pages of a book.Over the years, memoirs by politicians have revisited ideological battles, exposed differences within parties, offered personal accounts of political turning points and reopened controversies that many thought had been settled.From L K Advani's account of the Jinnah controversy to Jayaprakash Narayan's prison diary during the Emergency, these books have offered glimpses into the people and decisions behind some of India's defining political moments.Here are five political memoirs that made headlines for what their authors chose to reveal.When Natwar Singh's autobiography was released in 2014, much of the attention centred on his account of Sonia Gandhi's decision not to become prime minister in 2004.While Sonia had publicly described the decision as a call of her "inner voice", Singh offered a different explanation. He claimed that Rahul Gandhi had strongly opposed his mother's elevation, fearing that she could meet the same fate as her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, and mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, both of whom were assassinated.Singh wrote that Rahul's opposition was so strong that he gave Sonia 24 hours to decide. He also claimed that he, Manmohan Singh, Suman Dubey and Priyanka Gandhi were present when Sonia struggled with the decision. According to him, Rahul's intervention ultimately led her to offer the post to Manmohan Singh.The memoir went beyond the 2004 episode. Singh offered a sharply critical assessment of Sonia's leadership and her control over the Congress, describing her as increasingly authoritarian and secretive. He also recounted conversations with former prime minister P V Narasimha Rao, who, according to Singh, was troubled by Sonia's attitude towards him.The revelations triggered a political storm. Sonia rejected Singh's account and announced that she would write her own book. Former prime minister Manmohan Singh dismissed the claims as a "marketing gimmick", while the Congress accused Natwar Singh of distorting facts to promote his book.The controversy deepened when Singh made remarks linking Sonia's alleged ruthlessness to her Italian origin, drawing further criticism.Released in New Delhi on March 19, 2008, by then President A P J Abdul Kalam, L K Advani's autobiography traced his journey from childhood in Karachi and Partition to his association with the RSS, the growth of the BJP, the Ram Janmabhoomi movement and his years in the Union government.One of its most discussed sections revisited the controversy surrounding Advani's June 2005 visit to Pakistan and his remarks on Muhammad Ali Jinnah. During the visit, Advani praised Jinnah's August 11, 1947, address to Pakistan's Constituent Assembly, in which the latter spoke about religious freedom and equal citizenship irrespective of religion.The remarks triggered a backlash within the BJP and the Sangh Parivar. Sections of the party viewed them as a departure from its ideological position, and Advani eventually resigned as BJP president.Looking back at the episode, Advani described it as "simply the most agonising moment of my political life". He also recalled feeling let down by several party colleagues during the controversy, contrasting their response with the support he had received during the Hawala case in 1996.Explaining the purpose of his Pakistan visit, he wrote: "I went to Pakistan as a messenger of peace, with an earnest desire to contribute to the normalisation of relations between our two long-estranged nations."Advani maintained that he had not described Jinnah as secular but had referred to a particular speech as a "classic, a forceful espousal of a Secular State". He also argued that the media had reported his remarks without adequately explaining their historical context.The autobiography also revisited the 1990 Rath Yatra and the demolition of the Babri Masjid on December 6, 1992. Another section offered insights into his long association with former prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee.While acknowledging that the two sometimes differed in their approaches, Advani wrote that he had always regarded Vajpayee as his leader and generally deferred to his opinion.Published in January 2012 by Roli Books, Mamata Banerjee's My Unforgettable Memories offered a personal account of the relationships, disappointments and political rivalries that shaped her career. The English book was a translation of excerpts from her earlier Bengali writings.It appeared just months after Mamata led the Trinamool Congress to a historic victory in the 2011 West Bengal assembly elections, ending the Left Front's 34-year rule. Her observations about prominent political figures, particularly Sonia Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi, attracted considerable attention.Having spent years in the Congress before leaving the party to establish the Trinamool Congress in 1998, Mamata wrote about feeling repeatedly let down by its leadership. She referred to Sonia Gandhi as the "Queen Mother" and criticised the party's treatment of regional leaders."The culture in Congress is that when a regional faction gets too active, it's immediately censored by the top leadership," she wrote.Her account of Sonia, however, stood in contrast to the affection she expressed for Rajiv Gandhi, whom she described as "the leader of our hearts".Mamata recalled that after she was attacked at a rally in Kolkata in 1991 by alleged CPM activists, Rajiv took responsibility for arranging and paying for her treatment. He also sent people to ask whether she wanted to travel to the US for further medical care.She wrote that she was devastated when she heard of Rajiv's assassination in May 1991. She said she could neither eat nor speak to anyone for a week and described the loss as being "orphaned all over again, for the second time in my life since my father's death".The memoir also spoke warmly of former President Pranab Mukherjee, despite the changing political equations between the Congress and the Trinamool Congress."I have always respected him and my relationship with him is that of an elder brother and his kid sister," she wrote.She recalled that when Mukherjee was sidelined by the Congress and formed the Rashtriya Samajwadi Congress in 1986, she had repeatedly requested Rajiv Gandhi to take him back into the party.Unlike the other books, Jayaprakash Narayan's Prison Diary was not a retrospective account written years after the events. It was a record of his experiences during one of the most turbulent periods in India's democratic history: the Emergency.Popularly known as JP, Narayan was among the most prominent leaders of the movement against Indira Gandhi's government in the 1970s. His call for Sampoorna Kranti (Total Revolution) had brought together students, opposition parties and civil society groups.After the Allahabad high court set aside Indira Gandhi's election from Rae Bareli on June 12, 1975, the movement gathered momentum. On June 25, JP addressed a massive rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, calling for a peaceful struggle against the government. Hours later, the Emergency was proclaimed. In the early hours of June 26, opposition leaders, including JP, were arrested.Written during his detention and published by Popular Prakashan in 1977, the diary documented his experiences in custody, his health, his reading and his reflections on the political crisis.One of its most striking passages appeared in the opening entry, dated July 21, 1975, nearly a month after his arrest. JP wrote, "My world lies in a shambles all round me."He went on to express disbelief that a democratically elected prime minister could use the law to undermine democracy and suppress political opposition. The diary also contained sharp criticism of the decision to impose the Emergency, arrest opposition leaders and curtail civil liberties.Another deeply personal aspect of the book was its account of JP's deteriorating health. He was 72 when arrested and was already facing health problems. During his detention, his kidneys failed. He was released on November 12, 1975, on medical grounds and subsequently required regular dialysis for the remaining years of his life.Published in the year the Emergency ended and the Janata Party came to power, Prison Diary offered a contemporary first-person account of the political crisis from one of its most prominent opponents.Former President Pranab Mukherjee's The Presidential Years (2012-2017) made headlines even before its release in December 2020. The book offered his assessment of the Congress's decline, his dealings with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and some of the most consequential decisions taken during his presidency.Looking back at the Congress's defeat in the 2014 Lok Sabha elections, when the party won just 44 seats, Mukherjee attributed its performance to several factors, including its failure to recognise the end of its charismatic leadership. He described the establishment as having been reduced to a "government of averages".His observations also touched upon the Congress's leadership under Sonia Gandhi and Manmohan Singh.The memoir was equally candid about his interactions with Modi during his five-year tenure as President. Mukherjee described their relationship as cordial and said he had regularly offered the prime minister advice on policy matters. However, he criticised the NDA government's handling of Parliament between 2014 and 2019, blaming its "arrogance and inept handling" for the acrimonious exchanges between the treasury and opposition benches, while holding the opposition responsible too.One of the most discussed revelations concerned demonetisation. Mukherjee disclosed that Modi had not consulted him before announcing the decision on November 8, 2016. He said the lack of prior consultation did not surprise him, as the element of surprise was essential to such an announcement.He recalled that Modi visited Rashtrapati Bhavan after announcing the decision and explained its rationale. Mukherjee described demonetisation as a bold step but warned that it could cause a temporary economic slowdown and that the government would have to be careful about easing the burden on the poor.The memoir also became the subject of a family disagreement. Mukherjee's son, former Congress MP Abhijit Mukherjee, asked the publisher to halt publication until he had reviewed the final manuscript and given written consent. His daughter Sharmistha Mukherjee opposed the demand, saying their father had completed the manuscript before falling ill and that the final draft retained his handwritten notes and comments.Accusing her brother of creating "unnecessary hurdles", Sharmistha said preventing the book's release would be the "greatest disservice" to their departed father. The disagreement played out on social media, adding a family feud to the political conversations surrounding the memoir.Political memoirs offer a rare window into the personal experiences and perspectives of those who have occupied positions of power. They can reveal ideological differences, internal party dynamics and relationships that rarely find space in official accounts.But they are also personal interpretations of history. The authors decide which episodes to revisit, which conversations to disclose and how to explain decisions made years earlier. And, as the controversies surrounding these books show, sometimes what a politician writes long after leaving office can reopen debates that their public life had never quite settled.
Article Summary: Political memoirs often bring long-held views, personal accounts and contested versions of history back into the spotlight. From L K Advani's account of the Jinnah controversy to Jayaprakash Narayan's prison diary during the Emergency, these books have offered glimpses into the people and decisions behind some of India's defining political moments.

Article Title: BJP MP Ajeet Gopchade urges PM Modi to ensure representation of divyang persons in Parliament

Rajya Sabha MP Ajeet Gopchade has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi seeking an institutional mechanism for the representation of divyang persons in Parliament and state legislatures, citing examples of countries that have created such systems in their legislatures.The Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) has forwarded the letter to the ministry of home affairs and law ministry "for appropriate action".Gopchade, a BJP MP from Maharashtra, wrote to the prime minister on Sept 28, 2026, seeking examination of the feasibility of appropriate mechanisms for greater representation of divyang persons in Parliament, "including consideration of suitable candidates for nomination to the Rajya Sabha, within the existing constitutional framework".He suggested the creation of a transparent mechanism for "identifying persons with disabilities who have exceptional achievements, professional expertise, public-service experience and demonstrated leadership, so that their knowledge and lived experience can contribute to legislative and policy-making processes".Appreciating Modi govt's emphasis on dignity, inclusion and empowerment of differently-abled persons, including usage of the terminology 'divyang', Gopchade requested that their "representation in democratic institutions may also merit further consideration"."A Parliament that provides meaningful opportunities for capable persons with disabilities to participate in law-making can help bring diverse experiences and perspectives into the legislative process," he underlined, while highlighting examples of different countries that have created institutional mechanisms to facilitate the participation or representation of persons with disabilities in their legislatures.The letter cited the reservation of five parliamentary seats in Uganda for persons with disabilities, which are filled through special electoral colleges. In Japan, this category of persons has been provided an opportunity to participate in parliamentary proceedings, including through a special session involving its Upper House.In Zimbabwe, representation of differently-abled persons in the Senate is provided through a dedicated electoral mechanism. In Egypt, political parties are required to include candidates with disabilities in their electoral lists; while in Liberia a special constituency mechanism provides for their representation. In Namibia, a person with a disability was appointed to Parliament in 2005.Also recalling the noteworthy precedent in the Indian Parliament in Sadhan Chandra Gupta, a distinguished lawyer and politician who became the first visually-challenged MP, Gopchade noted: "His contribution demonstrates that disability need not be a barrier to distinguished legislative service".Though he did not cite more examples, sources close to Gopchade said Jaipal Reddy, a former Congress MP and Union minister, has been the last notable person with disability who has contributed immensely to parliamentary proceedings.Gopchade suggested that divyang persons be given representation in Parliament through the nominated MP route, as "many exceptionally capable divyang persons may face practical difficulties in participating in electoral politics and competing through conventional electoral processes"."This makes it worthwhile to examine whether appropriate constitutional, statutory and institutional mechanisms can be developed to facilitate their greater participation in Parliament and other legislative bodies," he said.The PMO, acknowledging Gopchade's letter, forwarded his suggestions to the ministry of law and justice and ministry of home affairs on October 29, 2026, "for appropriate action". While the matter relating to representation of persons in Parliament primarily pertains to the ministry of law and justice, the nomination of members to Rajya Sabha primarily pertains to the ministry of home affairs, as per the Govt of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961.
Article Summary: BJP MP Ajeet Gopchade has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi seeking an institutional mechanism for the representation of divyang persons in Parliament and state legislatures. He suggested the creation of a transparent mechanism for "identifying persons with disabilities who have exceptional achievements, professional expertise, public-service experience and demonstrated leadership" The PMO has forwarded the letter to the ministry of home affairs and law ministry "for appropriate action"

Gadchiroli/Nagpur: Hope has returned to India's erstwhile Maoist heartland where tribal families once despaired at the prospect of armed groups snatching children from their mothers, abducting daughters from their homes and preventing people from even voting, PM Narendra Modi told a gathering in Gadchiroli Sunday as he basked in the "countless blessings" showered on his govt for "defeating Maoism and Naxalism".Addressing the Janjatiya Gaurav Divas event through video-conferencing on the 151st birth anniversary of Birsa Munda, PM Modi said the size of the turnout was testimony to people's appreciation of the govt's effort to end Maoist depredations in 125 districts across the country."As far as my eyes can see, there are people everywhere...The sister who now feels safe is blessing us. The child whose childhood was once snatched away is today joining us as a young person. He is receiving opportunities for education and employment."PM Modi said, "In Chhattisgarh, areas like Bastar, where people were once afraid to go, I celebrated Diwali with our security forces." He said 170-odd tribal projects were inaugurated and more than 70 - together worth nearly Rs 3,000 crore - had been launched across states. Citing a World Bank report, he said nearly 50 crore people had escaped extreme poverty."I consider this one of the greatest achievements of the country since Independence. "PM said a British-era rule classifying bamboo as a tree and jailed tribals who cut it had finally been removed. "We re-classified bamboo as a variety of grass and ensured our tribal brothers and sisters have a right over it."He mentioned this during an online interaction with three tribals from Maharashtra, Gujarat and Telangana, blaming previous govts for the law surviving so long."After Independence, this mistake should have been corrected. But some people in those govts neither had an understanding of tribal society nor concern for it, and they kept that law running for years," he said.Vazirbhai Kotwalia, a bamboo artisan from Bharuch district, told Modi training had raised his monthly income from Rs 8,000 to Rs 25,000. Sabavat Anvesh of Telangana, now studying at IIT-Kanpur, told PM he looked forward to giving back to society after the opportunities he received. "I aspire to work on air pollution so that everyone can breathe clean air."Modi urged India's tribal people to commemorate Nov 15 every year on a bigger scale than before.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi: Hope has returned to India's erstwhile Maoist heartland. He basked in the "countless blessings" showered on his govt for "defeating Maoism and Naxalism" He said 170-odd tribal projects were inaugurated and more than 70 - together worth nearly Rs 3,000 crore - had been launched across states.

Article Title: Criminal killed in 5th 'encounter' in West Bengal since May
Article Text:
Ratan Sheikh encounter site

Nanoor/Kolkata: A history-sheeter in Bengal, who had allegedly shot and injured a constable on Nov 13, was killed by police Sunday, the fifth such "encounter death" in the state since BJP came to office in May.Ratan Sheikh, who had shot Santiniketan police constable Biswajit Das on his left knee to throw him off his trail, was gunned down at a desolate brick kiln at Nanoor after he fired at cops, police said.He had fled to Burdwan after shooting at constable Das.CM Suvendu Adhikari told reporters: "He (Sheikh) was a notorious criminal with 36 cases pending against him. If somebody fires at police, the latter will not shower flower petals on them or feed them batasha. Police have been given a free hand (to deal with these criminals). All goons should flee to Bangladesh, where there are Jamatis (fundamentalists). If they stay here, we will do what is necessary."

Article Title: CRPF men in anti-Naxal ops diverted to Manipur
Article Text:
A battalion comprising more than 1,000 personnel has been withdrawn

New Delhi/Raipur: CRPF has withdrawn a battalion comprising more than 1,000 personnel from the anti-Naxal operations theatre in Chhattisgarh and sent it to Manipur for deployment.The development marks the first such de-induction of any CAPF unit following Centre's declaration that Naxalism in India ended in March.Temporary withdrawal of companies (part of a battalion) has occurred for various internal security duties, such as the West Bengal elections, the Amarnath Yatra and protests in Delhi.Officials said the battalion was based in the former Maoist hotbed of Sukma. "This is the first full withdrawal of paramilitary unit from the anti-Naxal operations following the declaration that armed Maoism in the country ended in March," a security officer based in Delhi said.
Article Summary: CRPF has withdrawn a battalion from the anti-Naxal operations theatre in Chhattisgarh. The development marks the first such de-induction of any CAPF unit. Centre's declaration that Naxalism in India ended in March. The battalion was based in the former Maoist hotbed of Sukma.

Article Title: Launching new anti-anaemia strategy without enough evidence could waste public funds, warn experts
Article Text:
Experts are questioning India's push for double-fortified salt to fight anaemia, citing limited evidence and the risk of overlooking wider causes of iron deficiency. (AI-generated image)

From fortification of rice with iron, as the focus shifts to double fortification of salt (DFS) with iron and iodine in a bid to tackle high incidence of anaemia, several public health experts have sounded a warning against introducing any intervention without enough evidence. The new national anaemia prevalence data is yet to be made public though the survey was completed in November 2025.In response to an RTI application, the National Institute of Nutrition had stated in September that the analysis of the data from the Diet and Biomarkers Survey of India (DABS-I) launched in December 2022 and completed three years later is still under progress. The DABS-I survey, now renamed Survey for Assessment of Markers of Population Health, Activity, Diet and Anthropometry (SAMPADA), has used venous blood samples or samples drawn from veins, said to be the gold standard to estimate anaemia. DABS-I, which covers only 2.6 lakh people in the survey, will give state level prevalence, unlike NFHS with a sample size of seven lakh, which gives district-level data.However, with the data from the survey not being made public, India has no anaemia data since the last NFHS survey in 2019-21. That NFHS survey showed an increase in anaemia over the last survey in 2115-16. The government rejected the anaemia data from the 2019-21 survey on the grounds that it used blood samples drawn from the tip of the finger, which studies have shown to be unreliable.The Comprehensive National Nutrition Survey (CNNS) of 2016-18 used venous blood samples. It showed lower prevalence of anaemia than the 2019-21 survey which was attributed to using venous blood samples. DABS-I/SAMPADA’s anaemia data, comparable to the CNNS survey data, is expected to show even lower prevalence. It could show whether areas where distribution of iron fortified rice was done successfully have witnessed significant reduction in anaemia prevalence.Tamil Nadu was a pioneer in distributing DFS through the school midday programme starting from 2004. Within a few years, it was expanded to include the public distribution system (PDS) and Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS). Yet, the NFH surveys of 2015-16 and of 2020-21 showed that more than 50% children and women of all ages in the state were anaemic. Over a quarter had moderate anaemia, while 3.5% of women and 1.8% of children up to 5 years were severely anaemic. While Tamil Nadu’s anaemia incidence is low compared to many northern states, it is much higher than in states like Odisha, Jharkhand, Kerala and Andhra Pradesh, according to the CNNS survey. Almost 41% of children in the 1-4 year age group and over 20% in the 5-9 year age group were iron deficient in TN, which is higher than the national incidence, showed the CNN survey.In 2017, DFS distribution started in Uttar Pradesh. A study funded by the Gates Foundation was conducted in May 2020 to ascertain evidence of effectiveness in use of DFS in large-scale programmes. It found that only two (Etawah and Auraiya) of the five intervention districts met the evaluability threshold of 50% DFS utilization. The study found that there was no difference in anaemia and iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) prevalence or in mean haemoglobin concentration between women of reproductive age in intervention and comparison districts. It concluded that DFS was effective in reducing risk of iron deficiency, but not anaemia or iron deficiency anaemia, among women of reproductive age. Some of the modest efficacy was attributed to supply chain interruptions over the course of the implementation period.Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat introduced DFS in PDS and ICDS in 2018. Despite an impact evaluation claiming high DFS uptake exceeding 90% in the two states, the NFHS-5 survey, which took place from January 2020 to April 2021 in Madhya Pradesh, two years after introduction of DFS in June 2018, found that the overall prevalence of anaemia in children (aged 6 months to below 5 years) had increased from 69% in the previous NFHS survey to 73%, of which 42% were moderately anaemic, while 3% were severely anaemic. About 27% of adult women had moderate anaemia, and 2% had severe anaemia. However, a survey in March 2021 to gauge the impact of DFS introduction commissioned by an international NGO, Nutrition International, which supports the introduction of DFS, claimed that there was a six-percentage point reduction in anaemia prevalence in the districts where baseline prevalence had been measured in 2018. Nutrition International’s website states that it is working with state governments “to increase the availability of fortified foods in social safety net programs” which means publicly funded programmes, where poor purchasing power of the consumers would not be a hurdle to DFS uptake.There is enough evidence to show that only about half the cases of anaemia are due to iron deficiency. Anaemia can also be caused by malaria, hookworms and other such worm infestation, other nutritional deficiencies, chronic infections, and genetic conditions. Apart from these, it can be caused by socio-economic factors such as underage or early marriage, adolescent pregnancy, untreated excessive blood loss during menstruation and under-nutrition.Even the government’s targeted intervention to address anaemia among pregnant women by ensuring consumption of iron folic acid, distributed for free as supplements, has done poorly. Over half the pregnant women in India consumed iron and folic acid for 100 days and less than 38% consumed it for 180 days, according to the 2023-24 NFHS. In high fertility states like Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, the share of pregnant women who took iron and folic acid was even smaller.“Very little is being done to address food availability, diversity and affordability; minimum wages; equitable land distribution; better employment and job opportunities; or even to make nutrient dense foods available at low costs or as subsidies. Fortification will only increase food costs and dependence on corporations, while reducing the shelf life of foods and taking away food sovereignty from communities,” said Dr Sylvia Karpagam, a public health expert, and Dr Veena Shatrugna, former deputy director of the National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) and Steering Committee Member of the Right to Food Campaign, in a statement flagging the problems with the universal use of DFS in social safety net programmes such as ICDS and the midday meal scheme.The government has already spent about Rs 2,700 crore on rice fortification every year for several years. Public health experts cautioned against one more universal scheme that could waste thousands of crores of rupees of public funds, which could be utilised for more localised evidence-backed interventions.
Article Summary: Public health experts have sounded a warning against introducing any intervention without enough evidence. The new national anaemia prevalence data is yet to be made public though the survey was completed in November 2025. The government rejected the anaemia data from the 2019-21 survey on the grounds that it used blood samples drawn from the tip of the finger.

Article Title: Punjab BJP forms manifesto, 'chargesheet' committees; Raghav Chadha, Harbhajan Singh among members
Article Text:
Raghav Chadha and Harbhajan Singh feature in the BJP's manifesto panel as the party gears up for the 2027 Punjab polls

NEW DELHI: Punjab BJP president Kewal Singh Dhillon on Sunday constituted two committees ahead of the 2027 assembly elections, naming senior leaders to panels tasked with preparing the party's manifesto and a "chargesheet". Raghav Chadha and former cricketer Harbhajan Singh are among the members of the manifesto committee, which will be headed by senior BJP leader Avinash Rai Khanna.The panel also includes Manpreet Singh Badal, Ashwani Sharma, Manoranjan Kalia, Som Parkash, Rana Gurmeet Singh Sodhi, Ashwani Sekhri, Satnam Singh Sandhu, Rajinder Gupta, Parampal Kaur and HS Phoolka, according to a party statement.Former Punjab chief Sunil Jakhar will lead the chargesheet committee.Its members include Iqbal Singh Lalpura, Vijay Sampla, Shwet Malik, Maharani Preneet Kaur, Ravneet Singh Bittu, Dinesh Babbu, Sushil Rinku, Geja Ram, Vikramjit Singh Sahney, Ashok Mittal, Sandeep Pathak, SS Channi and Jagmeet Singh Brar.The BJP said the manifesto committee brings together experienced leaders from different fields to contribute to drafting its election document. Senior leaders in the chargesheet panel have also been assigned specific responsibilities.
Article Summary: Punjab BJP president Kewal Singh Dhillon names senior leaders to panels tasked with preparing the party's manifesto and a "chargesheet" Raghav Chadha and former cricketer Harbhajan Singh are among the members of the manifesto committee. Former Punjab chief Sunil Jakhar will lead the chargesheet committee.
